title: The Scientific Case Against Net Zero Falsifying the Greenhouse Gas Hypothesis

candidates.error_location: Section on IPCC radiative forcing, Eq. (3)–(4) and the numbers quoted for Figure 1
candidates.exact_quote:
Forcing (F) = 5.35Log(Cₜ/C₀)                                         (3)

and that temperature change is:

Delta(t) = Lambda x Delta(F)                                         (4)

Where Lambda is thought to be 0.4 to 0.5; Cₜ is the concentration (ppmv) and C₀ is the starting concentration (ppmv).

This gives Figure 1, which shows that between 400ppmv and 800ppmv of CO₂ the cumulative expected temperature change is 0.64°C (Lambda = 0.4) and 0.81°C (Lambda = 0.5)
candidates.claim_content: The paper uses the IPCC radiative forcing expression F = 5.35 Log(C_t/C_0) W/m^2, where C_t is the CO2 concentration in ppmv and C_0 is the starting concentration in ppmv, together with ΔT = λ·ΔF where λ is taken as 0.4–0.5 K/(W m^-2). From these it concludes that going from 400 ppmv to 800 ppmv gives ΔT = 0.64 °C for λ = 0.4 and ΔT = 0.81 °C for λ = 0.5. Check: the standard IPCC forcing formula is F = 5.35 ln(C/C_0) using the NATURAL logarithm, which gives ΔF = 5.35 × ln(2) = 3.708 W/m^2 and hence ΔT = 1.48 °C (λ=0.4) or 1.85 °C (λ=0.5). The quoted values 0.64 and 0.81 can only be reproduced by using log base 10: 5.35 × log10(2) = 1.610 W/m^2, × 0.4 = 0.644, × 0.5 = 0.805.
candidates.suspected_defect: The authors have interpreted 'Log' in the IPCC forcing equation as base-10 logarithm rather than the natural logarithm, understating the computed temperature change by a factor of ln(10) ≈ 2.303. All downstream numbers (0.64 °C, 0.81 °C, and the claimed '~0.81°C upper limit') are therefore too small by this factor.

candidates.error_location: Paragraph following Figure 1 discussion: 'The upper limit is ~0.81°C.'
candidates.exact_quote: show that there is an upper limit to the temperature change which can occur by adding ‘greenhouse gases’ to the atmosphere if the main source of incoming radiation (the Sun) does not change over time. The upper limit is ~0.81°C.
candidates.claim_content: Using F = 5.35·Log(C_t/C_0) and ΔT = λ·ΔF with λ ≤ 0.5, the paper computes ΔT ≈ 0.81 °C for a doubling of CO2 from 400 to 800 ppmv, and then asserts that 0.81 °C is an 'upper limit' on the temperature change achievable by adding greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.
candidates.suspected_defect: A logarithmic function is unbounded above; the same formula applied from 800 to 1600 ppmv gives another increment of equal size. A per-doubling increment cannot be an absolute upper limit. The conclusion does not follow from the stated equations.

candidates.error_location: Section 4 (costs), 'cost each household in the UK £78,000 ... £58,000 ... ~£300,000 per household in total'
candidates.exact_quote: is likely to cost each household in the UK £78,000 to decarbonise power generation and £58,000 to decarbonise road transport between now and 2050. With investment costs alone of £40bn per annum to 2050. All this expenditure, ~£300,000 per household in total
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that Net Zero will cost each UK household £78,000 to decarbonise power generation and £58,000 to decarbonise road transport between now and 2050, and then states that 'all this expenditure' totals ~£300,000 per household. The two itemised components sum to £136,000 per household.
candidates.suspected_defect: £78,000 + £58,000 = £136,000, which is less than half of the stated ~£300,000 per household total. No additional itemised components are given to account for the remaining ~£164,000, so the total is not derivable from the stated inputs.

candidates.error_location: Section 4 (costs): cross-check of per-household cost against national total
candidates.exact_quote: estimates of costs up to £1.4 trillion for the UK alone offset by £1.1 trillion potential but dubious savings giving a net cost of £321 billion (385.2bn USD)
candidates.claim_content: The paper states UK Net Zero costs of up to £1.4 trillion offset by £1.1 trillion of savings, giving a net cost of £321 billion. It also states a per-household cost of ~£300,000, which multiplied by roughly 28 million UK households gives ~£8.4 trillion, and £136,000 per household (the sum of the itemised £78,000 + £58,000) gives ~£3.8 trillion. Elsewhere the paper quotes 'circa £3 trillion or more' for decarbonising the energy system.
candidates.suspected_defect: (a) £1.4 trillion − £1.1 trillion = £0.3 trillion = £300 billion, not £321 billion. (b) The per-household figures, when scaled by the number of UK households, give totals (£3.8–8.4 trillion) that are mutually inconsistent with the £1.4 trillion gross and £321 billion net figures quoted in the same paragraph, and with the 'circa £3 trillion' figure quoted earlier.

candidates.error_location: Human Breathing paragraph
candidates.exact_quote: With 7 billion people breathing would produce ~0.1638ppmv of CO₂ in air. This can be calculated since the average resting adult produces 500g CO₂ per person per day (TOXNET) and will produce much more when active. This gives a baseline of 1.2775Pg per annum or 0.168% of the total or 0.1268ppmv resting and up to ~0.25ppmv CO₂ in air if most people are active.
candidates.claim_content: The paper computes human respiratory CO2 output: 500 g CO2 per person per day × 365 days × 7×10^9 people = 1.2775×10^15 g = 1.2775 Pg per annum, which is 1.2775/760 = 0.168% of the stated total annual CO2 emission rate of 760 Pg/yr. The paper elsewhere uses the conversion that 0.327 Pg CO2 ≈ 0.042 ppmv, 3 Pg ≈ 0.38 ppmv and 8 Pg ≈ 1.03 ppmv, i.e. approximately 7.8 Pg CO2 per ppmv. Applying this, 1.2775 Pg corresponds to 1.2775/7.8 = 0.1638 ppmv. The same sentence states both '~0.1638ppmv' and '0.1268ppmv resting'. Later the paper states that 10.4 billion people would produce ~0.24 ppmv resting and ~0.5 ppmv active.
candidates.suspected_defect: The two values given for the same quantity, 0.1638 ppmv and 0.1268 ppmv, are mutually inconsistent. 0.1638 ppmv is the value consistent with the paper's own Pg→ppmv conversion factor and with the later projection of 0.24 ppmv for 10.4 billion people (10.4/7 × 0.1638 = 0.243); 0.1268 ppmv is not. Correspondingly, the '~0.25ppmv ... if most people are active' figure is double 0.1268, not double 0.1638.

candidates.error_location: Anthropogenic CO2 calculation after Eq. (1) Ea(%) = 4.3%
candidates.exact_quote: That is, with 420ppmv CO₂ in air the total accumulated anthropogenic part is (4.3%) ~18ppmv (4.19ppmv p.a.) which is negligible
candidates.claim_content: The paper computes the anthropogenic share of annual CO2 emission flux as Ea/Er = 32.7 Pg per year / 760 Pg per year = 4.3%. It then multiplies this flux percentage by the atmospheric stock of 420 ppmv to conclude that 'the total accumulated anthropogenic part' of atmospheric CO2 is ~18 ppmv, and simultaneously states that anthropogenic emissions amount to 4.19 ppmv per annum.
candidates.suspected_defect: This is a dimensional/logical non sequitur: a fraction of an annual flux (Pg/yr) is applied to a stock (ppmv) to obtain an accumulated amount. Moreover the two numbers given are internally inconsistent with any plausible accumulation: at 4.19 ppmv per annum of anthropogenic emission, the accumulated anthropogenic contribution would exceed 18 ppmv after only ~4.3 years of emission, whereas emissions have continued for over a century. Also, 4.19 ppmv/yr of anthropogenic emission exceeds the observed annual atmospheric increase (~2–2.5 ppmv/yr implied by the paper's own '~120 ppmv over ~60 years'), which contradicts the claim that the anthropogenic contribution to the stock is negligible.

candidates.error_location: Logistics paragraph in the anthropogenic CO2 section
candidates.exact_quote: Logistics: 8Gt CO₂ (Alzard et al., 2019; Schwanen et al., 2011; Tacken et al., 2014) (i.e. 8Pg/year, ~25% from man-made sources or ~1% of total CO₂ in air) ~1.03ppmv CO₂ is due to logistics.
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that logistics emits 8 Gt CO2 = 8 Pg/year, which it describes as '~25% from man-made sources or ~1% of total CO₂ in air', and equivalent to ~1.03 ppmv of CO2 in air. The paper's stated total anthropogenic emission is 32.7 Pg/yr and total emission from all sources is 760 Pg/yr; total atmospheric CO2 is 420 ppmv.
candidates.suspected_defect: '~1% of total CO₂ in air' is wrong: 8/760 = 1.05% of total annual emissions from all sources, not of the atmospheric stock. As a fraction of the atmospheric stock, 1.03 ppmv / 420 ppmv = 0.25%. The 1% figure confuses a flux fraction with a stock fraction.

candidates.error_location: Burning Fossil Fuels paragraph
candidates.exact_quote: Burning Fossil Fuels: 10,000million tonnes of CO₂ (i.e. 10Pg), ~1.28ppmv CO₂ is due to burning fossil fuels (Parker & deBaro, 2019).
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that burning fossil fuels emits 10,000 million tonnes of CO2 (10 Pg/yr) equivalent to ~1.28 ppmv, while in the immediately preceding paragraph it states that logistics alone emits 8 Pg/yr (~1.03 ppmv) and earlier that total anthropogenic emission is 32.7 Pg/yr. It also states that the UK alone emits 0.327 Pg which is 1% of anthropogenic emissions.
candidates.suspected_defect: Internal inconsistency: fossil-fuel combustion (10 Pg) is stated to be smaller than the paper's own total anthropogenic emission (32.7 Pg) while logistics (8 Pg), which is essentially fossil-fuel combustion, is stated to be 80% of the fossil-fuel total and only 25% of the anthropogenic total. These three figures cannot all be mutually consistent.

candidates.error_location: Equations (1) and (2), Ideal Gas Law section, definition of R
candidates.exact_quote: R = gas constant (m³ K⁻¹ mole⁻¹ kg) = 8.314
candidates.claim_content: The paper defines the Molar Mass version of the Ideal Gas Law as T = PM/(ρR), with T in Kelvin, P the near-surface atmospheric pressure in kPa, M the mean molecular weight, ρ the near-surface density in kg m^-3, and R the gas constant stated as 8.314 with units 'm³ K⁻¹ mole⁻¹ kg'.
candidates.suspected_defect: The stated units of R are dimensionally wrong. The universal gas constant is 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1 = 8.314 kg m^2 s^-2 mol^-1 K^-1 = 8.314 m^3 Pa mol^-1 K^-1. 'm³ K⁻¹ mole⁻¹ kg' has dimensions of volume·mass per mole per Kelvin and cannot make T = PM/(ρR) dimensionally consistent. Also the units of M are not given (they must be g mol^-1 if P is in kPa for the numerical values to come out right).

candidates.error_location: Ideal Gas Law / Table 1 discussion
candidates.exact_quote: The average near-surface temperature for planetary bodies with an atmosphere calculated from the Ideal Gas Law is in excellent agreement with measured values suggesting that the greenhouse effect is very small or non-existent (Table 1).
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims that the formula T = PM/(ρR), derived by rearranging PV = nRT, predicts near-surface planetary temperatures in excellent agreement with observation, and that this agreement constitutes evidence that the greenhouse effect is very small or non-existent. Here P is measured surface pressure, M is mean molar mass, ρ is measured near-surface atmospheric density, and R is the gas constant.
candidates.suspected_defect: T = PM/(ρR) is an algebraic identity (a rearrangement of the ideal gas law), not an independent prediction: the density ρ is itself a function of T at given P and M, and in practice is tabulated using the measured T. Agreement with observation is therefore guaranteed by construction and carries no information about radiative effects. The inference from the identity to the non-existence of a greenhouse effect is circular.

candidates.error_location: Discussion of Coe et al. (2021) and the Beer–Lambert law
candidates.exact_quote: Most of the temperature change has already occurred and increasing CO₂, CH₄, N₂O concentrations will not lead to significant changes in air temperatures because absorption is logarithmic (Beer-Lambert Law of attenuation) – a law of diminishing returns.
candidates.claim_content: The paper asserts that absorption of infrared radiation by CO2, CH4 and N2O is logarithmic in concentration, and attributes this logarithmic dependence to the Beer–Lambert law of attenuation. The Beer–Lambert law states that transmitted intensity I = I_0 exp(-ε c l), i.e. absorbance A = ε c l is LINEAR in concentration c and the absorbed fraction 1 - exp(-ε c l) saturates exponentially toward 1.
candidates.suspected_defect: The Beer–Lambert law gives absorbance linear in concentration and absorbed fraction approaching saturation exponentially, not logarithmically. The approximately logarithmic dependence of radiative forcing on CO2 concentration arises from the shape of the pressure/Doppler-broadened absorption line wings of a saturated band, and is not a consequence of Beer–Lambert alone. The stated justification does not follow from the law cited.

candidates.error_location: Discussion of CO2 residence time and the 'Principle of Equivalence'
candidates.exact_quote: The residence time of CO₂ in the atmosphere is between 3.0 and 4.1 years using the IPCC's own data and not the supposed 100 years or 1000 years for anthropogenic CO₂ suggested by the IPCC summaries for policy makers (Harde, 2017) which contravenes the Equivalence Principle
candidates.claim_content: The paper computes the residence time of CO2 in the atmosphere as the atmospheric stock divided by the gross annual exchange flux (stock ≈ 420 ppmv ≈ 3280 Pg CO2, gross flux 760 Pg/yr, giving ~4 years), and asserts that this contradicts the longer adjustment timescales (100–1000 years) cited by the IPCC, claiming the IPCC assigns different residence times to natural and anthropogenic CO2 molecules in violation of a 'Principle of Equivalence'.
candidates.suspected_defect: Mathematically, the turnover (residence) time of an individual molecule in a reservoir with large bidirectional exchange fluxes is not the same quantity as the e-folding decay time of a perturbation to the reservoir's total content. In a two-box model with large gross exchange and small net imbalance, the molecular turnover time can be a few years while the perturbation relaxation time is centuries. The paper's argument conflates the two, so the inferred contradiction and the asserted violation of equivalence do not follow.

candidates.error_location: Discussion of Coe et al. (2021) climate sensitivity
candidates.exact_quote: The result is that climate sensitivity to doubling concentration of CO₂ is (0.5°C) including 0.06°C from CH₄ and 0.08°C from N₂O which is so small as to be undetectable.
candidates.claim_content: The paper reports that the calculated climate sensitivity to a doubling of CO2 is 0.5 °C, stated as 'including 0.06°C from CH₄ and 0.08°C from N₂O'. A climate sensitivity to CO2 doubling is by definition the response to doubling CO2 alone and cannot 'include' contributions from doubling other gases.
candidates.suspected_defect: The arithmetic/definitional structure is incoherent: if 0.5 °C is the sensitivity to CO2 doubling, it cannot include 0.06 °C from CH4 and 0.08 °C from N2O; if it does include them, the CO2-only sensitivity would be 0.36 °C. The quoted figures are mutually inconsistent as stated.

candidates.error_location: Keeling curve paragraph
candidates.exact_quote: shows a very gentle increase of ~120ppmv over the last ~60 years
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that the Keeling Curve of CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa shows an increase of ~120 ppmv over the last ~60 years. The Mauna Loa record began in 1958 at approximately 315 ppmv; the paper elsewhere states the present concentration as 'circa 420ppmv'.
candidates.suspected_defect: Using the paper's own figure of 420 ppmv today and the 1958 starting value of ~315 ppmv, the increase over ~60–66 years is ~105 ppmv, not ~120 ppmv. The quoted increase is inconsistent with the paper's own stated current concentration.

candidates.error_location: Paragraph citing Skrable et al. (2022)
candidates.exact_quote: Skrable et al., (2022), show that accumulated human CO₂ is 11% of CO₂ in air or ~46.84 ppmv based on modelling studies.
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that accumulated human CO2 is 11% of atmospheric CO2, equal to ~46.84 ppmv. Elsewhere the paper takes atmospheric CO2 to be 420 ppmv.
candidates.suspected_defect: 11% of 420 ppmv = 46.2 ppmv, not 46.84 ppmv; 46.84 ppmv corresponds to 11% of 425.8 ppmv. The two figures are not consistent with the 420 ppmv value used elsewhere in the paper. Additionally, 46.84 ppmv (11%) contradicts the paper's own earlier conclusion that accumulated anthropogenic CO2 is ~18 ppmv (4.3%), a figure the paper endorses in the same paragraph.

candidates.error_location: Kinetic theory paragraph
candidates.exact_quote: there are 10³⁴ collisions between air molecules per second per cubic meter of gas at a pressure of 1 atmosphere (~101.3kPa)
candidates.claim_content: The paper asserts that at 1 atmosphere (~101.3 kPa) there are 10^34 collisions between air molecules per second per cubic metre. Standard kinetic theory gives the total collision rate per unit volume as Z = (1/2) n^2 σ <v_rel>, with n ≈ 2.5×10^25 m^-3 at STP, collision cross-section σ ≈ 4.3×10^-19 m^2, and mean relative speed <v_rel> ≈ 600 m/s.
candidates.suspected_defect: The quoted order of magnitude should be checked: Z = 0.5 × (2.5×10^25)^2 × 4.3×10^-19 × 600 ≈ 8×10^34 collisions m^-3 s^-1, i.e. closer to 10^35 than 10^34. Possible order-of-magnitude slip, though only by a factor of ~8.

candidates.error_location: Paragraph on water vapor attribution
candidates.exact_quote: the IPCC's attribution of 80% of warming to water vapor (~5% in air) and 20% to CO₂ (~0.04% in air)
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that water vapour constitutes ~5% of air and CO2 ~0.04% of air. The global mean water vapour mixing ratio in the atmosphere as a whole is approximately 0.25% by volume (about 0.4% near the surface on average), reaching ~4% only in the warmest, most humid surface conditions.
candidates.suspected_defect: The '~5% in air' figure for water vapour is an upper local/surface extreme, not a global atmospheric concentration, and overstates the global mean by more than an order of magnitude. This number is used to support subsequent quantitative claims about the relative importance of water vapour and CO2.

candidates.error_location: Paragraph on COVID and 1970s oil crisis emission reductions
candidates.exact_quote: Noting that two periods in recent times reduced human CO₂ emissions by as much as 20% (covid 2020–2023 and 1970s oil crisis) yet the Keeling curve (figure 2) shows no evidence of that effect
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims that human CO2 emissions were reduced 'by as much as 20%' during COVID (2020–2023) and the 1970s oil crisis, and that the Keeling curve shows no evidence of such a reduction. Global fossil CO2 emissions fell by approximately 5.4–7% in 2020 relative to 2019 and recovered in 2021.
candidates.suspected_defect: The 20% reduction figure substantially overstates the actual reduction (~6–7% for one year). Moreover, even a 20% reduction in an annual emission of ~4 ppmv/yr would reduce the annual atmospheric increment by only ~0.8 ppmv, which is at or below the level of interannual natural variability in the growth rate — so the absence of a visible step in the Keeling curve does not constitute the evidence the argument claims.

candidates.error_location: Figure 1 axis description
candidates.claim_content: Figure 1 is described with a vertical axis (Delta T, °C) running from 0 to 0.9 and a horizontal axis (CO2 concentration, ppmv) running from 0 to 1000, plotting ΔT = λ·5.35·Log(C/C_0) for λ = 0.4 and λ = 0.5. The text states that between 400 and 800 ppmv the cumulative change is 0.64 °C (λ=0.4) and 0.81 °C (λ=0.5).
candidates.suspected_defect: If the curves pass through ΔT = 0.81 °C at 800 ppmv (λ = 0.5), then at 1000 ppmv the same formula gives ΔT = 0.5 × 5.35 × log10(1000/400) = 1.06 °C, which exceeds the stated maximum of the vertical axis (0.9 °C). The plotted range and the quoted values appear mutually inconsistent.

candidates.error_location: Ideal Gas Law section, concluding sentence
candidates.exact_quote: The ideal gas law is robust and works for all gases.
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that the ideal gas law PV = nRT 'works for all gases', while in the same section defining n as 'the number of moles of a real gas' and applying the law to Venus's atmosphere, which is described in the table note as '96.5% supercritical carbon dioxide' at ~9.2 MPa and ~740 K.
candidates.suspected_defect: The ideal gas law is an idealisation valid in the dilute limit; real gases deviate measurably at high pressure, and supercritical CO2 at ~92 bar (as the paper itself describes Venus's atmosphere) departs significantly from ideality. The blanket claim that it 'works for all gases' is false and the Venus calculation in particular is applied outside the regime where the ideal gas law is accurate.
